name: JavaScript Basics
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Modern JavaScript: let and const, coercion, functions and closures, array methods, destructuring and spread, modules and the DOM.

lesson.intro: JavaScript runs in every browser and, through Node.js, on servers too, so nearly every software engineer reads and writes it. This lesson covers the modern core of the language: declaring variables, types and the coercion rules that surprise newcomers, template literals, functions and closures, the array methods you'll use daily, objects with destructuring and spread, modules, and a short tour of the DOM.
objectives: Choose between const and let and explain block scope and hoisting
Predict the result of coercion with +, - and ==, and compare with === instead
Write arrow functions and closures, and transform arrays with map, filter and reduce
Unpack and copy objects and arrays with destructuring, spread, ?. and ??
Split code into ES modules and update a page through the DOM safely

sections.title: Declaring variables: let, const and var
sections.body:
Open any modern codebase and you'll see `const` almost everywhere, `let` occasionally and `var` almost never. The reasons come down to two questions: can this name be reassigned, and where is it visible?
- `const` declares a name that can't be reassigned, and it must get a value immediately. It protects the binding, not the value: a const array or object can still be changed with `push` or by setting a property.
- `let` declares a name you can reassign, such as a counter or a running total.
- `var` is the pre-2015 way. It behaves differently in ways that cause bugs, so modern code avoids it.

`let` and `const` are **block scoped**: a name declared inside `{ }` (an if block, a loop body, a function) exists only inside those braces. A `let` inside a block with the same name as an outer variable creates a separate variable that shadows the outer one.

`var` is **function scoped**: it ignores blocks, so a var declared inside an if or a loop leaks out into the whole function. var declarations are also **hoisted**: the declaration moves to the top of its function but the assignment stays put, so reading a var before its line gives `undefined` instead of an error. `let` and `const` are hoisted too, but reading them before their declaration throws a ReferenceError. That stretch before the declaration is called the **temporal dead zone**, and an error there is far better than a silent undefined.

The rule most teams follow: use `const` by default, switch to `let` only when you actually reassign, and don't use `var`. Code then documents itself: if you see `let`, you know the value changes somewhere below.

Never assign to a name you haven't declared. In old-style scripts that silently creates a global variable; in modules and strict mode it throws a ReferenceError.
sections.pitfall: Assuming const makes a value read-only. It only stops reassignment; use `Object.freeze()` if you truly need an object that can't change.

check.question: You need a loop counter that goes up by one on each pass. Which declaration fits best?
check.explanation: The counter is reassigned, so const would throw. let allows reassignment and stays inside the loop block, while var leaks out of it and an undeclared name creates an accidental global.

sections.title: Types, coercion and equality
sections.body:
`"5" + 1` is `"51"` but `"5" - 1` is 4. If that looks random, it's because JavaScript converts types automatically, and the rules are learnable.

JavaScript has seven primitive types: `number` (all numbers, as 64-bit floats), `string`, `boolean`, `undefined` (a value never set), `null` (deliberately empty), `bigint` and `symbol`. Everything else, including arrays and functions, is an object. `typeof x` reports the type as a string, with two famous quirks: `typeof null` is `"object"` and so is `typeof []`. Use `x === null` and `Array.isArray(x)` for those checks.

**Type coercion** is JavaScript converting a value to another type on its own:
- `+` with a string on either side converts the other side to a string and joins them: `"5" + 1` is `"51"`.
- `-`, `*` and `/` only work on numbers, so they convert strings to numbers: `"5" - 2` is 3 and `"6" * "2"` is 12.
- A string that isn't a number becomes `NaN` (Not a Number), which then spreads through any arithmetic. NaN is the only value not equal to itself, so test for it with `Number.isNaN(x)`.

Convert explicitly when data comes in. `Number("42")` gives 42 but `Number("12px")` gives NaN, while `parseInt("12px", 10)` reads digits until something else appears and gives 12. `String(42)` goes the other way.

`==` (loose equality) converts types before comparing, so `0 == ""` is true and `null == undefined` is true. `===` (strict equality) never converts: different types are simply not equal. Always use `===` and `!==`. The one exception some teams allow is `x == null`, which checks for null and undefined at once.

In conditions, every value is truthy or falsy. The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `"false"`, `[]` and `{}`.
sections.code:
console.log("5" + 1);          // 51  (string join)
console.log("5" - 2);          // 3   (numeric)
console.log("6" * "2");        // 12
console.log("abc" * 2);        // NaN
console.log(typeof 42, typeof "hi", typeof null);   // number string object
console.log(Number("12px"), parseInt("12px", 10));  // NaN 12

console.log(0 == "", 0 === "");                     // true false
console.log(null == undefined, null === undefined); // true false
console.log(Boolean("0"), Boolean([]), Boolean("")); // true true false
sections.pitfall: Doing math on values from text inputs, JSON or URLs without converting them. `"4" + "5"` is `"45"`, so call `Number()` first.

sections.title: Strings and template literals
sections.body:
Building a message by gluing strings with `+`, as in `name + " has " + count + " new messages"`, gets ugly fast, and one missing space ruins it. **Template literals** fix this.

A template literal is written with backticks instead of quotes. Inside it, `${expression}` inserts the value of any expression: a variable, arithmetic, a function call or a ternary. Template literals can also span multiple lines and keep the line breaks exactly as written, which is handy for messages and small HTML snippets.

Strings are immutable, just like in Python, so every method returns a new string:
- `s.length` (a property, not a method) gives the number of characters.
- `s.toUpperCase()`, `s.toLowerCase()` and `s.trim()` clean up text.
- `s.includes("x")`, `s.startsWith("http")` and `s.endsWith(".js")` answer yes or no questions.
- `s.slice(start, end)` takes characters from start up to but not including end. Negative numbers count from the end, so `s.slice(-3)` is the last three characters.
- `s.split(",")` breaks a string into an array, and `arr.join(", ")` joins an array back into a string.
- `s.replace("a", "b")` replaces the first match, and `s.replaceAll("a", "b")` replaces every match.
- `s.padStart(2, "0")` pads on the left, which is useful for times and IDs: `"7".padStart(2, "0")` is `"07"`.

Compare strings with `===`, which is case sensitive, so normalize with `toLowerCase()` before comparing what a user typed. `s[0]` reads a character, but assigning `s[0] = "X"` silently does nothing, because strings can't change.

The ternary operator `condition ? a : b` pairs naturally with template literals for small choices such as plurals: `${count} item${count === 1 ? "" : "s"}`.
sections.pitfall: Using quotes instead of backticks. `"Hi ${name}"` prints the dollar sign and braces literally; only backtick strings interpolate.

check.question: What string does the template literal `${2 + 3} apples` produce?
check.explanation: Everything inside ${ } is evaluated as JavaScript, so 2 + 3 becomes 5 before it is inserted. You would only see the literal ${2 + 3} if the string used quotes instead of backticks.

sections.title: Functions, arrow functions and closures
sections.body:
JavaScript gives you three ways to write a function, and you'll see all three in real code.
- A **function declaration**: `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`. Declarations are hoisted completely, so you can call them above the line where they're written.
- A **function expression** assigns a function to a variable: `const add = function (a, b) { ... };`. Like any const, it can't be used before its line.
- An **arrow function**: `const add = (a, b) => a + b;`. With no braces, the arrow returns its expression automatically. With braces, it's a normal body and needs `return`. A single parameter needs no parentheses (`n => n * 2`), and returning an object literal needs parentheses around it: `() => ({ ok: true })`.

Arrow functions are the default for short callbacks such as `items.map(x => x.id)`. One real difference: arrows don't have their own `this`; they use the `this` of the surrounding code. That's what you want in callbacks, but it makes arrows a poor choice for object methods that rely on `this`.

Parameters can have defaults, as in `function greet(name = "friend")`, and a **rest parameter** such as `...nums` collects any remaining arguments into a real array. Calling a function with too few arguments isn't an error in JavaScript: missing parameters are simply `undefined`.

Functions are values, so they can be passed around and returned. When a function is created inside another function, it keeps access to the outer function's variables even after the outer function has returned. That's a **closure**. Closures let you keep private state, such as a counter that only the returned function can change, and they explain a classic bug: callbacks created in a loop over a `var` all share one variable, while `let` gives each iteration its own binding.
sections.pitfall: An arrow function with braces but no `return`: `n => { n * 2 }` returns undefined. Drop the braces or add return.

check.question: Given const double = n => n * 2; what does double(4) return?

sections.title: Arrays and map, filter, reduce
sections.body:
You have a list of orders and need the total of the paid ones, or a list of users and need just their emails. In JavaScript you'll rarely write an index-based `for` loop for this, because arrays come with methods that each express one idea.

Basics first. Arrays are zero-indexed, `arr.length` is the count, `arr.push(x)` adds to the end, `arr.pop()` removes from the end, `arr.includes(x)` checks membership and `arr.at(-1)` reads the last item. `for (const item of arr)` loops over the items.

The core methods each take a callback that's called once per item:
- `map(fn)` returns a **new array** of the same length, with each item transformed.
- `filter(fn)` returns a new array with only the items for which fn returns something truthy.
- `find(fn)` returns the **first** matching item, or `undefined` if none match.
- `some(fn)` and `every(fn)` return true or false.
- `reduce(fn, initial)` combines all items into one value. The callback receives the running result (the **accumulator**) and the current item, and returns the new accumulator. Always pass the initial value: without it, reduce starts from the first item and throws on an empty array.
- `forEach(fn)` just runs the callback and returns `undefined`; use it only for side effects.

Because map and filter return arrays, you can chain them: `orders.filter(o => o.paid).map(o => o.total)` reads like a sentence.

Two traps with `sort()`. It sorts **in place** and returns the same array. And without a compare function it converts items to strings and sorts them as text, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. For numbers, pass a compare function: `(a, b) => a - b` sorts ascending, because a negative result puts a first. To sort without changing the original, copy first with `[...arr].sort(...)`.
sections.pitfall: Calling `sort()` on numbers without a compare function. The default sorts as text, so 100 comes before 9.

check.question: What does [3, 1, 2].map(n => n + 1) return?
check.explanation: map returns a new array with the function applied to each item, in the same order: 3 + 1, 1 + 1, 2 + 1. It does not sort or sum anything.

sections.title: Objects, destructuring and spread
sections.body:
Most data in JavaScript programs is objects: a user from an API, a settings bundle, a database row. Working with them fluently means knowing a handful of syntax shortcuts that appear in nearly every modern file.

An object literal groups named properties: `{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }`. Read a property with dot notation (`user.name`) or brackets (`user["name"]`); brackets are needed when the key is in a variable, as in `user[field]`. Reading a missing property gives `undefined`, not an error. `Object.keys(obj)`, `Object.values(obj)` and `Object.entries(obj)` give arrays you can loop over. When a variable already has the property's name, the **shorthand** `{ name, age }` means `{ name: name, age: age }`.

Objects and arrays are held by reference. `const b = a` makes b point at the same object, so a change through b shows through a, exactly as in Python.

**Destructuring** unpacks values into variables:
- Objects by name: `const { name, age } = user;`. Rename with `{ name: who }` and give defaults with `{ role = "guest" }`. A default only applies when the value is undefined.
- Arrays by position: `const [first, second] = list;`, and `[a, b] = [b, a]` swaps two variables.
- It works in parameters too: `function show({ name, age }) { ... }` reads like named arguments.

**Spread** (`...`) expands an array or object in place:
- `[...a, ...b]` joins arrays, and `[...a]` copies one.
- `{ ...defaults, ...options }` merges objects. Later properties win, which makes this the standard way to apply overrides.
- These copies are **shallow**: nested arrays and objects are still shared.

Two operators make missing data safer. **Optional chaining** `user.address?.city` gives undefined instead of throwing when address is null or undefined. **Nullish coalescing** `value ?? fallback` uses the fallback only for null or undefined, unlike `||`, which also replaces 0 and empty strings.
sections.pitfall: Treating a spread copy as a deep copy. `{ ...obj }` copies only the top level, so nested objects are still shared. Use `structuredClone(obj)` for a deep copy.

check.question: What does b hold after const { a, b = 5 } = { a: 1, b: null }?
check.explanation: Destructuring defaults only apply when the value is undefined. null is a real value, so b is null. The same rule applies to default parameters, while ?? treats null and undefined alike.

sections.title: Modules: import and export
sections.body:
A real project has dozens or hundreds of files. Modules are how they share code without everything landing in one giant global scope.

An **ES module** is a file whose top-level variables are private to that file by default. To share something, you `export` it; to use something from another file, you `import` it.
- **Named exports**: `export function add(a, b) {...}` or `export const PI = 3.14;`. A file can have many. Import them by their exact names in braces, `import { add, PI } from "./math.js";`, and rename with `as`: `import { add as plus } from "./math.js";`.
- A **default export**: `export default function Button() {...}`. A file has at most one, and the importer picks any name, without braces: `import Button from "./Button.js";`.
- `import * as math from "./math.js"` gathers every named export into one object.

Paths starting with `./` or `../` are relative to the current file. A bare name like `"react"` refers to an installed package, which a bundler such as Vite or webpack (or Node itself) resolves from `node_modules`.

Imports are **live, read-only bindings**: you can call and read what you imported, but assigning to an imported name throws. `import` declarations must sit at the top level of the file, not inside an if or a function. When you need to load code conditionally or lazily, the `import()` function returns a promise for the module.

In the browser, a file is treated as a module only when loaded with `<script type="module" src="app.js">`. Modules always run in strict mode and wait until the HTML has been parsed.

You'll also meet Node's older format, CommonJS: `const fs = require("fs")` and `module.exports = {...}`. Newer Node code uses ES modules (files ending in .mjs, or "type": "module" in package.json). The idea is the same either way: explicit exports, explicit imports.
sections.pitfall: Mixing up default and named imports. `import area from "./math.js"` asks for the default export, not the named `area`; named exports need braces.

check.question: A variable is declared at the top level of an ES module without export. Where can it be used?
choices: Anywhere, because it becomes a global variable
In every module that imports anything from that file
Only after another module calls require on the file
check.explanation: Each module has its own top-level scope. Only exported names are visible to other modules, and only to those that import them.

sections.title: The DOM, briefly
sections.body: When a browser loads a page, it turns the HTML into a tree of objects called the **DOM** (Document Object Model). JavaScript changes what's on screen by changing that tree, and it reacts to the user by listening for **events**. Frameworks like React do this for you, but they are built on exactly these calls, and knowing them makes framework code far less mysterious. Finding elements: `document.querySelector("#total")` returns the first element matching a CSS selector, or null if none matches, and `document.querySelectorAll(".item")` returns all matches. Changing elements: - `el.textContent = "..."` sets the text. It treats the value as plain text, so it's safe for anything a user typed. - `el.classList.add("active")`, `.remove()` and `.toggle()` change CSS classes, which is the clean way to change appearance. - `el.value` reads or sets what's in an input box, and it's always a string. - `document.createElement("li")` makes a new element, and `parent.append(child)` puts it on the page. Reacting to the user: `button.addEventListener("click", handler)` runs handler each time the button is clicked, passing an **event** object with details such as `event.target` (the element) or `event.key` for keyboard events. For forms, listen for `"submit"` and call `event.preventDefault()` to stop the browser reloading the page. The handler doesn't run right away; it runs later, whenever the event happens. The JavaScript Async topic explains how the browser schedules it. Security matters even in small projects. `el.innerHTML = userText` parses the text as HTML, so a comment containing an `` tag can run code in other users' browsers. That's cross-site scripting (XSS). Use `textContent` for text, and keep innerHTML for markup you wrote yourself. Put your script tag at the end of the body or give it the `defer` attribute (modules are deferred automatically), so the elements exist before your code looks for them.
sections.pitfall: Using `innerHTML` with text a user typed. It runs any HTML inside the text, which opens the door to XSS; use `textContent`.

check.question: A script in the page's head calls document.querySelector("#add") and gets null, though the button exists in the HTML. What is the most likely cause?
choices: querySelector needs a dot before ids
Buttons can't be selected by id
The script ran before the button was parsed; add defer or move the script to the end of the body
The DOM is only available inside event listeners
check.explanation: A plain script runs as soon as the browser reaches it, before the rest of the HTML is parsed. defer (or type="module") waits until the document is ready. # is the correct prefix for ids.

keyTerms.definition: let and const exist only inside the braces where they are declared.
Declarations are processed before code runs; var reads as undefined early, let and const throw.
JavaScript converting a value to another type automatically, as in "5" + 1 giving "51".
Compares value and type without any conversion; use it instead of ==.
A value that acts as false: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN.
A backtick string that inserts ${expression} values and can span lines.
A compact function, (a, b) => a + b, that returns its expression and has no own this.
A function that keeps access to variables from the scope where it was created.
Unpacking object properties or array items into variables, as in const { name } = user.
... that expands an array or object, used to copy, join and merge (shallowly).
A file with its own scope that shares code through export and import.
The browser's tree of objects representing the page, changed through JavaScript.

summary: Use const by default and let when you must reassign; avoid var, which is function scoped and hoisted as undefined.
+ with a string concatenates while -, * and / convert to numbers; compare with ===, never ==.
Template literals with backticks and ${} replace string concatenation.
Arrow functions return their expression when written without braces, and closures keep access to outer variables.
map, filter and reduce return new values; sort mutates and compares as text unless you pass (a, b) => a - b.
Destructuring, spread, ?. and ?? handle objects concisely; modules share code with export and import, and the DOM is changed with querySelector, textContent and addEventListener.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: const stops you from pointing arr at a different array, but push changes the existing array in place, which is allowed. The TypeError only happens on a reassignment such as arr = [].

questions.question: This code throws an error. Why?
choices: for...of loops cannot declare their variable with const
count must be declared with var to be used inside a loop
count is const, so count = count + 1 is a reassignment and throws a TypeError
A number variable cannot count the items of a string array
questions.explanation: Reassigning a const throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable, so count should be declared with let. The const in for...of is fine because each pass creates a new binding for item.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: var declarations are hoisted to the top of the script or function, but the assignment stays where it is. So total exists but has no value yet. With let or const the same code throws a ReferenceError.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: When either side of + is a string, + joins text. The number 1 becomes "1" and the result is the string "51", not the number 6.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: - only works on numbers, so the string "5" is converted to 5 and the result is the number 3. Only + switches to joining strings.

questions.question: Which comparison evaluates to false?
questions.explanation: === never converts types, and null and undefined are different types, so it is false. The other three use ==, which coerces: null and undefined are loosely equal to each other, and "" and "1" become the numbers 0 and 1.

questions.question: Which of these values is truthy?
questions.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, even "0". The number 0, the empty string and NaN are all on the falsy list. It is the string's length that matters, not what it says.

questions.question: Complete the arrow function so makeUser("Ada") returns the object { name: "Ada" }.
questions.explanation: Parentheses tell JavaScript the braces are an object expression to return. Without them, { name: name } is read as a function body containing a label, so the function returns undefined. { return name } returns the string, not an object.
questions.concept: returning an object from an arrow function

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: Each call to makeCounter creates a new count variable. a has been called three times by the time it is logged, so it returns 3; b has its own count and returns 1 on its first call. Separate calls of the outer function do not share state.

questions.question: This code should log 0, 1, 2 but logs 3, 3, 3. What is the fix?
choices: Use a longer delay so the loop has time to finish
Replace the arrow function with a regular function
Declare i with let so each iteration gets its own i for the callback to close over
questions.explanation: var creates one i for the whole loop. The callbacks run after the loop ends, when that shared i is 3. let creates a fresh binding on every iteration, so each callback remembers its own value. Changing the function style or the increment does not change how many i variables exist.

questions.question: Complete the code so total is the number 12.
questions.code:
const prices = [{ price: 5 }, { price: 7 }];
const total = prices.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, _____);
questions.explanation: The accumulator must start as the number 0 so each step adds numbers. Starting with "" or [] turns + into string joining and gives "57", and starting with prices[0] adds to an object, giving "[object Object]7".

questions.question: What array does this expression return?
questions.explanation: filter keeps the even numbers, giving [2, 4], then map multiplies each by 10. Chained methods run left to right, each on the array returned by the previous one.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: b = a copies the reference, so a and b point to the same object, and changing b.score changes the one object both names see. Changing a property of a const object is allowed; only reassigning the variable throws.

questions.question: This throws instead of logging undefined. Why?
choices: console.log can't print values declared with let
city must be declared with const instead
city is in its temporal dead zone until its declaration runs, so reading it earlier throws ReferenceError
questions.explanation: let and const are hoisted but not initialized, and reading them before the declaration line throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'city' before initialization. Only var reads as undefined early.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: The inner let x is a separate variable that exists only inside the if block. It shadows the outer x there, but the outer x is still 1 when it's logged.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: Both are famous quirks. typeof null is "object" because of a bug kept for compatibility, and arrays are objects. Check with x === null and Array.isArray(x) instead.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: Number("") is 0, a surprise worth remembering when validating input. Number ignores surrounding spaces, so "  7 " is 7. parseInt reads digits until it hits something that isn't one, stopping at the dot, so it gives 3.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: Each ${ } is evaluated before insertion, so items * 2 becomes 6. Backticks are what make the placeholders work.

questions.question: Complete the line so the date string is broken into its three parts.
questions.explanation: split breaks a string at each separator and returns an array, here ["2024", "03", "09"]. slice takes a substring, join is an array method that does the opposite, and splice is an array method that edits in place.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: slice starts at index 1 (e) and stops before index 3, so it takes e and l. Like Python slices, the end index is excluded.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: sum() uses the default first = 0, and rest is an empty array, so 0 + 0 = 0. sum(5, 1, 1) sets first to 5 and gathers the remaining two arguments into rest, so 5 + 2 = 7.

questions.question: This logs undefined instead of 16. Why?
choices: Arrow functions can't use the * operator
n must be wrapped in two sets of parentheses
square must be declared with the function keyword
With braces, the body needs an explicit return; write n => n * n or add return
questions.explanation: Braces turn the arrow's body into a block, and a block without return returns undefined. The concise form n => n * n returns the expression automatically.

questions.question: What happens when this runs?
choices: It logs hi, then throws a ReferenceError for wave
It throws a ReferenceError before logging anything
questions.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their bodies, so greet works before its line. wave is a const holding an arrow function, and it's in the temporal dead zone until its line runs, so calling it early throws.

questions.question: What array does this log?
questions.explanation: Without a compare function, sort converts items to strings and compares them as text: "1" < "100" < "25" < "5". Pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numbers by value.

questions.question: Complete the compare function so the scores sort from highest to lowest.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.code:
const config = { retries: 0 };
console.log(config.retries ?? 3, config.retries || 3, config.timeout?.ms);
questions.explanation: ?? only falls back for null or undefined, so 0 is kept. || falls back for any falsy value, so 0 becomes 3. config.timeout is undefined, and ?. stops there and gives undefined instead of throwing.

questions.question: math.js only has a named export. Complete the import in app.js.
questions.explanation: Named exports are imported by name inside braces. import add from ... asks for the default export, which this file doesn't have. * as add would make add an object holding the exports, so add(2, 3) would fail.

questions.question: Which statements about ES modules are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Each module has its own top-level scope
A file can have many named exports but at most one default export
The importing file can reassign an imported name
Browsers load a file as a module only with <script type="module">
import declarations can go inside an if block
questions.explanation: Imported names are read-only bindings, so reassigning one throws. import declarations must be at the top level; use the import() function to load code conditionally.

questions.question: Which line safely shows a user's comment as text on the page?
questions.explanation: textContent treats the value as plain text, so any tags in it are displayed, not run. The other three parse the comment as HTML, which lets a malicious comment run script in other users' browsers (XSS).

questions.question: Complete the line so the handler runs when the button is clicked.
